title: The Felling and Transport of the Pine and Fir
text: THE pine and the fir are among the most useful foresttrees which the world produces. There is scarcely a dwelling welling or or a a ship shi to be found in any part of Europe or America into the building of which one of these varieties of wood does not enter; and the juices or resinous products are particularly valuable in the arts of life. Many nations, too, procure edible substances from various parts of these trees. All the varieties of the pine and the fir genera belong to one botanical order; but without entering into a description of the trees themselves, or their relation to botany or agriculture, we may collect many instructive details respecting the geographical distribution of the pine and fir forests the mode of felling and bringing to market -the economical uses of the timber, branches, bark, &c. and the mode of obtaining the resinous products.

The forests of Norway and Sweden are among the most celebrated of the pine and fir kind, the Scotch pine and the spruce fir being the principal varieties. Dr. E. D. Clarke says, "If the reader will cast his eyes on the map of Sweden, and imagine the Gulf of Bothnia to be surrounded by one continuous unbroken forest, as ancient as the world, consisting principally of pine-trees, with a few mingling specimens of the birch and juniper, he will have a general and tolerably correct notion of the real appearance of the country." A common mode of transporting these trees from the forests where they are cut down, to the banks of streams or rivers, is to place them on wheel-axles, one vehicle to each tree, and then to draw them by horses guided by women. In every case a path or road is taken which will lead by the shortest route to a river-such a river, in Sweden, is the Gotha, which enables the rafts of timber to be floated down to the port of Gottenburgh. There are in Norway two rivers thus employed: one, the Glomm, which terminates at Christiania; and the other, the Drammen, which flows into the sea twenty miles westward of Christiania.

Nearly all the pine and fir timber grown in Russia, Prussia, and Poland is floated down the rivers which flow into the Baltic, generally adjacent to the ports of Memel, Dantzig, Riga, and St. Petersburg. The name of the port is often given to the kind of timber which is floated down to it: thus we hear of 'Riga timber' and Memel timber.' It is said that the timber shipped at Memel comes principally from the estates of Prince Radzivil, in Polish Prussia; it is more abundant than that shipped at any other of the Baltic ports; but its quality is inferior to that of Dantzig; while this latter, again, yields the palm of superiority THE 1843.] to the timber from Riga. This latter-named largely used for the masts of English and French sels; and in reference to it Mr. M'Culloch "The mast-trade is very extensive. The burghers Riga send persons, who are called 'mast-brokers,' the provinces to mark the trees, which are purchased standing. They grow mostly in the districts border on the Dnieper, and are sent up that river landing-place, whence they are transported thirty (about twenty-three miles) to the Dwina, where, formed into rafts of from fifty to one hundred pieces each, they descend the stream to Riga. The tree produces the longest masts is the Scotch pine. pieces, which are from eighteen inches to twentyinches in diameter, are called 'masts;' and those these dimensions spars,' or, in England, 'Norway masts, because Norway exports no trees more eighteen inches in diameter. Great skill is required in distinguishing those masts which are sound those which are in the least degree internally decayed They are usually from seventy feet to eighty feet length."

Mr. Howison has given a very interesting account the train of operations whereby Russian pine and are conveyed to St. Petersburg for shipment. As the large timber near the capital has long since cut down, the supply is obtained from a distance the interior. A Russian proprietor wishing to dispose of the timber on his property, having completed a gain with the St. Petersburg merchant, sets his santry to work in picking out, cutting down, dragging the trees from the forests to the lakes rivers. This work generally takes place during winter months, in order that everything may be for floating the timber to St. Petersburg as soon the ice on the rivers and lakes breaks up. As ground is generally covered several feet deep snow, and the trees judged to be sufficiently large sound for the foreign market lie widely apart, workmen and others employed in picking them are compelled to wear snow shoes, to prevent from sinking in the snow. When the trees are found they are cut down with hatchets, and the head branches lopped off. The trunk is then stripped of bark, and a circular notch is cut round the narrow of it, to facilitate the fixing of the rope by which the horses are to drag the trunk along; and a hole is made we at the other end for a handspike, to steer the log over the many obstacles that lie in its way. Many of these the trees are seventy feet in length, and of proportionate diameter; and they are drawn by from five to nine port horses each, yoked in a straight line one before another, since the intricate narrow paths in the woods will not permit of their going in any other way. One the man mounts upon the leading horse, and another upon of the middle one, while others support and guide with handspikes the large and distant end of the tree, to year raise it over the elevations of snow, and make it glide a smoothly along. The conveyance of these large trees, the the long line of horses, and the number of peasants on accompanying them through the forests, present a very picturesque appearance. In many cases the trees are brought nearly a thousand miles before they are delivered to the merchant; and they generally remain This under his care another winter, to be shaped and fitted for exportation in such a manner as to take up as little room as possible on shipboard; so that the Russian timber does not reach the foreign consumer till two years after it has been cut down. When the trees are delivered to the merchant, ant, they are carefully examined The to ascertain their soundness, and for this purpose a hatchet is struck several times against them, the emitted sound affording the means of estimating the soundfeet ness of the tree. The author of being An Autumn near the Rhine' says, "A little below Andernach the village of Namedy appears on the left which The Rhine here bank under a wooded mountain. The forms a little bay, where the pilots are accustomed to five unite together the small rafts of timber floated down under the tributary rivers into the Rhine, and to construct enormous floats, which are navigated to Dordrecht than (Dort), and there sold. These machines have the apfrom pearance of floating villages, each composed of twelve or fifteen little wooden huts, on a large platform of oak . and deal timber: they are frequently eight or nine in hundred feet long, and sixty or seventy in breadth." This raft is composed of several layers of trees, placed of one on another, and tied together, the raft drawing not fir less than six or seven feet of water. Several smaller all rafts are attached to the large one, besides a string of been in boats loaded with anchors and cables, and used for the purposes of sounding the river and going on shore. bar- The rowers and workmen sometimes amount to seven peaor eight hundred, superintended by pilots; and over and the whole is a proprietor or manager, whose habitation and is superior to the others. The "domestic economy" of the the raft is very complete. Poultry, pigs, and other ready animals are to be found on board, and several butchers are attached to the suite. A well-supplied boiler is at as work night and day in the kitchen. The dinner-hour the with is announced by a basket stuck on a pole, at which signal the pilot gives the word of command, and the and the workmen run from all quarters to receive their raout tions. The consumption of provisions during the them voyage from Andernach to Dort is enormous, some- , times amounting to forty or fifty thousand pounds of and bread, eighteen or twenty thousand pounds of fresh its meat, with salt meat, butter, vegetables, and a host of end et ceteras. A very large capital is necessary to undertake the formation of one of these rafts. When we proceed southerly towards Switzerland, find pine and fir forests elevated so much above level of the rivers, as to give occasion for no small exercise of ingenuity in devising the means of trans- . A remarkable instance of the plan, now frequently adopted, was afforded by M. Rupp about thirty years ago, in reference to the means of transporting wood from the forests on Mount Pilate to the Lake Lucerne. The mechanism has been so often described, that a slight notice will suffice here. In the 1810 the price of Baltic timber was so high, that hope was entertained of bringing into profitable sale timber on this Swiss mountain, hitherto untouched account of the difficulty of conveyance. M. Rupp conceived the idea of making an inclined plane whith should extend the whole distance from the top of the mountain to the Lake of Lucerne, about eight miles. inclined plane consisted of a trough, formed of twenty-five thousand pine-trees, six feet broad, and from three to six feet deep. To preserve a regular slope, it had to be conducted over the summits of rocks, along their sides, through tunnels, and over deep gorges, where it was sustained by scaffolding. trough was kept constantly moist, and the trees descended along it into the lake with extraordinary rapidity. The larger pine-trunks, about a hundred in length, descended through the whole distance eight miles in six minutes; a rapidity which pro- D2 duced an effect otherwise almost inconceivable to the view of a bystander. When the trunks arrived at the lake, they were floated down the Rhône to the sea. As the war, which occasioned the high price of Baltic timber, led to the construction of the Slide of Alpnach (as the contrivance was called), so did the return of peace restore the timber-trade to its old channel; and the Swiss project is understood not to have succeeded as a commercial speculation.

In many of the Alpine districts between Austria and Italy the difficulty of transporting timber to the level of the rivers has led to the construction of slides or troughs somewhat similar to that of Alpnach. In all such cases the slides are formed of several fir-trees placed side by side, and smoothed by being stripped of their bark: they are always made in such a direction as to maintain a pretty uniform slope. The slides are chiefly made use of in winter, at which time they are rendered more slippery by being wetted with water, which freezes immediately. A wood-cut and descrip- tion of one of these Tyrolean districts have been given in No. 532.

In Scotland, one of the principal pine-forests is said to be that of Rothiemurchus, which spreads over the glens and valleys of the Grampian Hills. The timber from this forest is generally floated down the river Spey; and when, from a long season of drought, or any other cause, there is any difficulty in getting it down to the river, the workmen collect the trees into a suitable dell, and having built up a temporary dam. they wait the coming of a flood, which in a country of such varied surface is no rare occurrence the temporary dam is full of water, they break down . As soon as the boundary, and the liberated waters, bursting from their confinement, carry the trees with them impe- tuously down the Spey.

Every one who has heard of States must be aware that the pine and fir forests cover Canada and the United a vast area of the new continent. Among the remark- able features of Canada, the lumbering-parties' are not the least picturesque. These are clubs or bands of men who form a kind of joint-stock tree-cutting com- pany,' and undergo no few hardships in the course of their labours. The proceedings of these lumberingparties have been fully described by an eye-witness, in our No. 352.
